newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan wants higher profile at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Japan wants higher profile at G7 summit.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto goes to this month's Group of Seven summit determined to keep Tokyo's profile high at a meeting likely to be less dominated by economics than in the past.

As Asia's only standard-bearer at the summit of industrialised countries, Hashimoto also has the task of making sure the region's voice is heard in a forum where, because of Russia's full formal participation for the first time, the emphasis is expected to be on Europe.

Japanese officials said the June 20-22 summit was expected to spend only one afternoon discussing economic issues during the three-day gathering of the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan.

"Japan will be reminded that Asia and Japan are not a central focus of this meeting as other G7 leaders are more interested in NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation), the Mideast and Africa," said Rei Shiratori, professor at Tokai University.
But Japan is not likely to be kept on the fringe of the discussions.

Hashimoto has much to say about the sweeping reforms he is carrying out to Japan's social, economic and financial systems to try to end a reputation for blocking free competition which has resulted in high prices of goods and services.
The other G7 members are also likely to zero in on Japan's growing trade surplus and a series of financial scandals.
Japan's trade surplus more than doubled in April and it is expected to have increased substantially in May after a sustained period of decline.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has said Japan's trade surplus is not on the leaders' agenda, but a sustained increase could hurt global growth and has the potential to create a protectionist backlash.
The issue may be taken up by President Bill Clinton when he meets Hashimoto on the sidelines of the summit.
Hashimoto will also come under pressure to dispel concern about a series of recent scandals in Japan's financial system.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has said the scandals involving Japan's major securities house Nomura Securities Co Ltd and leading bank Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd may have caused a loss of confidence in the Japanese system.

"Faced with those financial scandals and the fact that Japan has just come up with a financial reform plan, the prime minister may make an international pledge to quicken reforms," said a senior official of his ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
Japanese officials said once economic issues were out of the way, Hashimoto hoped to give Japan a higher profile at his second G7 summit by unveiling proposals on key global issues.
"Japan will be showing a more positive commitment to global issues and will make new proposals in many areas," said a senior government official.
The proposals include aid to promote development in Africa, and measures on anti-terrorism, nuclear energy safety and environmental preservation.

"The only way Japan can be an honourable member of the G7 is to positively take up issues such as the environment, human rights and democracy which it has been reluctant to do in the past," Shiratori said.
